issues.legal_issue: When the government resumes separately assessed property, the owner ceases to be liable for the revenue assessed on it unless the compensation included the value of abatement and the owner agreed to continue paying that revenue.
material_facts: The ferries were recognized as property, and their revenue had been separately assessed.
The government resumed the ferries and paid compensation calculated by reference to their collections after resumption.
The correspondence did not show that the compensation included the capitalized value of revenue abatement or that the owner agreed to keep paying the revenue assessed on the ferries.
The owner’s predecessors continued to pay the revenue under threat of coercive collection, and the court found no basis to draw an adverse inference from delay in seeking abatement.
issues.conclusion: The owner ceased to be liable for the separately assessed revenue on the resumed ferries; the compensation did not establish that the owner had agreed to continue paying it.
issues.legal_principle: A ferry right is a property right, as discussed in Nityabhari Ray and Others v. Dunne and Others. Regulation I of 1793, Regulation XIX of 1816, and Regulation VI of 1819 form part of the historical framework for assessment and resumption. Where property carrying a separate revenue assessment is resumed, liability for that assessment ceases unless there is evidence that compensation accounted for the abatement and that the owner accepted continued liability.

rule.if: resumption_case and revenue_separately_assessed and assessed_property_resumed and not evidence_compensation_included_abatement and not owner_agreed_to_continue_payment

predicates.resumption_case: The proceeding concerns a claim arising from the government’s resumption of property.
predicates.revenue_separately_assessed: The government had separately assessed revenue on the property.
predicates.assessed_property_resumed: The government resumed the property on which the revenue had been assessed.
predicates.evidence_compensation_included_abatement: The record contains evidence that the compensation included the value of abatement of the revenue.
predicates.owner_agreed_to_continue_payment: The owner agreed to continue paying the revenue assessed on the resumed property.
predicates.liability_for_resumed_property_revenue_c: The owner is no longer liable for revenue separately assessed on property resumed by the government.

issues.definition: When a resumption case concerns separately assessed property that the government resumed, the owner’s liability for its revenue ceases if there is no evidence that compensation included abatement and the owner did not agree to continue paying.

issues.legal_issue: A claim to recover revenue collected in excess of what was due is timely for payments within the applicable limitation period, while a claim for a declaration of abatement is not barred merely by delay where each government demand gives rise to a fresh cause of action.
material_facts: The owner sought recovery of revenue collected in excess of the amount due and a declaration that the revenue liability had abated.
The trial court awarded recovery for payments made during the three years before the suit and declared that liability for the revenue on the ferries had ended.
The record did not show that the claim for abatement had been refused before the suit.
The government had made demands and collected revenue on successive occasions.
issues.conclusion: The recovery claim was maintainable for payments made within the applicable limitation period, and the declaratory claim was not barred by limitation; each government demand gave rise to a fresh cause of action.
issues.legal_principle: A right to collect revenue that is not due cannot be acquired by prescription. A claim to recover an improper payment may be brought within three years of that payment, and each demand for recovery by the government creates a fresh cause of action. There is no limitation bar to the claim for a declaration of the right to abatement on the facts of this case.

rule.if: revenue_recovery_and_declaration_case and excess_revenue_paid and payments_within_limitation_period and government_demands_repeated and abatement_claim_not_previously_refused

predicates.revenue_recovery_and_declaration_case: The proceeding seeks recovery of revenue collected and a declaration concerning abatement of the revenue liability.
predicates.excess_revenue_paid: The owner paid revenue in excess of the amount lawfully due.
predicates.payments_within_limitation_period: The payments for which recovery is sought were made within the applicable limitation period before the claim was brought.
predicates.government_demands_repeated: The government made successive demands for the revenue.
predicates.abatement_claim_not_previously_refused: The government had not refused the abatement claim before the suit was brought.
predicates.timely_refund_claim_and_declaration_not_: The refund claim is timely for payments within the applicable limitation period, and the declaratory claim is not barred by limitation.

issues.definition: If an owner brings a revenue-recovery and declaration proceeding after paying excess revenue, the payments are within the applicable limitation period, government demands were repeated, and abatement had not previously been refused, the refund claim is timely and the declaration is not barred.

issues.legal_issue: Civil courts have jurisdiction over a suit seeking abatement of separately assessed revenue after the government resumes the property, where the applicable law does not expressly or impliedly exclude that jurisdiction.
material_facts: The suit sought abatement of revenue separately assessed on ferries resumed by the government.
The statutes and administrative rules relied on did not expressly exclude civil-court jurisdiction over the abatement claim or indicate that such jurisdiction was impliedly excluded.
The State relied on a prior decision concerning a challenge to the adequacy of compensation, which the Court distinguished from the claim in this suit.
issues.conclusion: The civil court had jurisdiction to hear the claim for abatement and the declaration that revenue was not payable on the resumed ferries.
issues.legal_principle: Section 9 of Regulation XIX of 1816 did not exclude civil-court jurisdiction over a claim for abatement of separately assessed revenue. Regulation VI of 1819 and Act I of 1866 likewise did not exclude jurisdiction over this claim; Act I of 1866 did not apply to the earlier resumptions. Rule 159 of the Bengal Tauzi Manual, 1940, did not establish an exclusion, even assuming it was statutory. Secretary of State for India in Council v. Maharajadhiraja Kameshwar Singh Bahadur concerned a different kind of compensation claim and did not govern this suit.

predicates.civil_suit_for_revenue_abatement: The proceeding is a civil suit seeking abatement of revenue assessed on property resumed by the government.
predicates.no_express_jurisdictional_bar: No applicable law expressly bars civil courts from hearing the claim.
predicates.no_implied_jurisdictional_exclusion: The applicable statutory and administrative scheme does not indicate that civil-court jurisdiction is impliedly excluded.
predicates.civil_court_has_jurisdiction: A civil court may hear the claim for abatement of revenue.

issues.definition: A civil court has jurisdiction over a revenue-abatement suit when no applicable law expressly or impliedly excludes its jurisdiction.
